readerTitle: The bins weren't the problem: asking why five times
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 청소 업체, 회계팀, 사내 개발팀) · 기법의 기원(Toyota)은 짧게만 언급하고 사례는 THK-07-09에서 다룸
insight: 첫 번째 '왜'의 답은 대개 사람을 가리키고, 다섯 번째 '왜'의 답은 고칠 수 있는 절차를 가리킨다.
misconception: 문제가 다시 생기면 실수한 사람을 바꾸거나 다시 교육하면 해결된다.

sources.text: Ohno, T. (1988). Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production. Productivity Press. (다섯 번의 '왜' 기법 설명)

factChecks.note: '다섯 번의 왜'가 Toyota 생산 방식에서 널리 알려졌고 오노 다이이치(Taiichi Ohno)가 저서에서 설명했다는 점을 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 기원을 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
청소 업체, 회계팀, 개발팀 사례와 원인 사슬은 모두 설명용 가상 사례입니다. 실제 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The bins weren't emptied. Again.
body: You run an office cleaning company. A client emails: the bins on the third floor were full on Friday morning. Third week in a row.
You already spoke to the cleaner after the first complaint. He apologized. It happened anyway.

image.label: An overflowing office bin beside an empty, tidy desk
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 저녁의 깔끔한 사무실, 책상 옆 쓰레기통만 넘쳐 있음. 벽 달력에 금요일 세 칸에 빨간 표시. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you do about the third complaint?
body: The client is annoyed but not leaving yet. You have one week to make sure it doesn't happen a fourth time.

options.text: Move a more reliable cleaner onto that building
options.feedback: It feels decisive and shows the client you acted. But if the cause isn't the person, the new cleaner will hit the same wall.

options.text: Give every cleaner a sign-off checklist for each floor
options.feedback: A checklist catches missed tasks, which helps. It doesn't tell you why a task gets missed, so the bins may just become a ticked box that's still full.

options.text: Ask why the bins were missed, then keep asking why about each answer
options.feedback: It takes a few conversations instead of one decision. In return, you find a cause you can fix once. The next card shows where it led.

cards.title: Follow the chain of whys.

breakdown.label: Why were the bins full?
breakdown.detail: The cleaner ran out of time on Thursday nights.

breakdown.label: Why only Thursdays?
breakdown.detail: A new client was added to his Thursday route last month.

breakdown.label: Why wasn't his time changed?
breakdown.detail: Routes are planned from contract hours, not from visiting the site.

breakdown.label: Why are hours set without a visit?
breakdown.detail: Sales quotes new jobs from floor size alone.

breakdown.label: Why does sales work alone?
breakdown.detail: Operations was never part of the quoting process.

cards.callout: The first answer pointed at a person. The fifth pointed at a process you can change.

cards.title: Ask why five times
body: **Asking why five times** means taking each answer to "why did this happen?" and asking why again, until you reach a cause that, once fixed, stops the problem coming back.
That deeper cause is called the **root cause**. The first answers are usually symptoms. The idea became well known through Toyota's factories, which a later lesson covers.
Five is a rule of thumb. Sometimes three whys are enough. Sometimes you need seven.

image.label: A plant with leaves labeled symptoms and roots labeled causes
image.brief: 식물 단면 인포그래픽. 땅 위 잎에는 "Full bins", "Late cleaner", 땅 아래로 내려갈수록 "Thursday route", "Planning by contract hours", 가장 깊은 뿌리에 "Quoting without operations". 뿌리 끝을 강조.

cards.title: Three habits make the whys useful.
body: The questions are easy. These habits keep the answers honest.
list: **Start with one specific fact:** "bins full on Friday," not "service is bad"
**Check each answer:** look at the route sheet or the quote before moving on
**Stop at something you control:** a fix you can make that prevents the next case
cards.callout: Here, the fix was simple: operations now visits every new site before the quote is sent.

cards.title: When the answer is a person, ask once more.
body: The finance team at a large company pays a supplier twice. Why? A clerk entered the same invoice twice. Most reviews stop here, with a warning to the clerk.
One more why: the supplier sent the invoice by email and by post. And another: the payment system doesn't flag a repeated invoice number.
Turn on that check and the mistake can't happen again, whoever is at the desk. People make errors. Good processes catch them.

image.label: Two identical invoices meeting at a checkpoint that stops one
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 똑같은 송장 두 장(하나는 봉투, 하나는 이메일 아이콘)이 컨베이어를 따라오고, "Duplicate check" 게이트에서 한 장이 멈춤. 사람은 작게 뒤편에.

cards.title: One chain can hide other causes.
body: Most problems have more than one cause. A single line of whys picks one path and can miss the rest. When answers branch, follow each branch a step or two.
It's also easy to steer the chain toward the answer you already believed. Check each step against facts, not memory.
And keep the tone curious. If the questions feel like blame, people give safe answers instead of true ones.

cards.title: Now it's a software team inside a large company.
body: Your team's weekly app release keeps slipping by a day. You've asked why three times: releases are late because testing finishes late, and testing finishes late because another team books the shared test environment on Thursdays.

options.text: Ask the other team to book fewer Thursday slots
options.feedback: It may buy you a few weeks. But it treats a scheduling clash, not the reason two teams fight over one environment.

options.text: Ask why both teams share one test environment, and whether that reason still holds
options.feedback: This costs one more conversation with the platform team. It may reveal that a second environment is cheap now, which ends the clash for good.

options.text: Add a manager sign-off so releases are planned earlier
options.feedback: It looks like control, but it adds a delay and blames planning. The environment is still booked on Thursdays.

cards.title: Keep asking why until the answer is a fix, not a culprit.
body: The first answer tells you who was there. The deeper answers tell you what to change so it doesn't happen again.
**Try it today:** pick one problem that has happened at least twice. Write it as a single fact, then write five whys underneath. Check one answer against real records.
